newsitem.title: USA: U.S. condemns closure of Belgrade radio station.
newsitem.headline: U.S. condemns closure of Belgrade radio station.

text.p: The United States condemned the closure on Tuesday of an independent radio station by Serbian authorities and called for a concerted international campaign against Belgrade's "anti-democratic" actions.

State Department officials listed measures they said would stay in force until Serbia changed its ways but made clear they had no plans at present to seek to re-impose full trade sanctions on Belgrade lifted by the United Nations last year.

Staff at Belgrade's only independent radio station, B-92, said the Serbian government shut it down as opposition street protests continued against President Slobodan Milosevic over alleged fraud in recent local elections.
"The United States condemns this suppression of the remaining elements of the independent media in Serbia," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

"This is a transparent effort to keep the Serbian public in the dark. It demonstrates the fundamental lack of respect, lack of regard the Serbian government has for democratic principles," Burns told a news briefing.

He said it was "curious indeed" that Milosevic's socialist government saw the radio's reports as a threat to itself. "This is a rather dim and dark picture of the corner into which the Serbian government has painted itself," he added.

The U.S. spokesman called again on Belgrade to respect the results of Nov. 17 elections which it had "flagrantly overturned" after they showed widespread victories for the opposition Zajedno coalition.

U.S. charge d'affaires Richard Miles had contacted Zajedno leaders over the last two days, including Vuk Draskovic, Zoran Djindjic and Vesna Pesic, Burns said, commending the group for keeping the demonstrations peaceful.

Despite the strong words, Burns made clear that U.S. action would be limited for now to pressing for worldwide condemnation of Serbian tactics and maintaining an existing "outer wall" of American sanctions on Belgrade.
"We are concentrating our efforts on trying to make sure that the entire international community is speaking out together uniformly about these anti-democratic measures in Serbia," he said.
A conference on Bosnia in London on Wednesday would stress forcefully to Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic that the annulment of the elections was unacceptable, he said.

Existing U.S. measures against rump Yugoslavia -- Serbia and Montenegro -- include: denial of full diplomatic ties, economic aid and trade preferences; a veto on Belgrade sitting in the United Nations and other organisations; and blockage of loans from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.

The measures would remain in force "as long as this type of (Serbian) behaviour continues", Burns said, adding that Washington had also told the European Union it was "not the time" to extend trade privileges to Serbia.

In Geneva, U.S. officials said on Tuesday that Washington had withdrawn its invitation to the Serbian government to attend high-level talks there this week aimed at enhancing economic cooperation in southeast Europe.
Burns noted that ever since U.N. sanctions on Serbia were lifted after last year's Dayton peace accords on Bosnia, the United States had reserved the right to seek their resumption.
But he said it would be "quite a complicated process" to have the Security Council reimpose them. "I'm not aware of any action to do so in the next week or two or three," he said.

Other officials acknowledged that Russia, which opposed the U.S. line on Serbia at this week's European security summit in Lisbon, was unlikely to go along. "I don't think we're heading in that direction," one said.
Burns told reporters the United States was "very disappointed" that Russia had insisted on striking out a call for Serbian democracy from the final declaration in Lisbon.
